Input

is capped at **1,048,576 bytes (1 MiB) of UTF-8** and is never truncated —
a file over the cap is rejected outright.

Under `--

exit 0
{
 "valid": true,
 "file": ".mcpjam/evals/s_billing.yaml",
 "suite": { "id": "s_billing", "name": "Bi
: \".mcpjam/evals/s_billing.yaml\",\n \"stage\": \"contract\", // \"contract\" is exit 1; \"input\" and \"parse\" are e

xit 2
 "findings": [
 {
 "code": "SUITE_FILE_INVALID", // or SUITE_FILE_TOO_LARGE / _EMPTY / _YAML_INVALID / _
MULTIPLE_DOCUMENTS\n \"path\": [\"cases\", 1, \"id\"], // field path as segments\n \"pointer\": \"cases[1].id\",
// the same path, rendered\n \"message\": \"duplicate case id \\\"c_refund\\\"\"\n // `location` accompanies SUITE_

n}
```

Findings are deterministically ordered and carry no timestamps, so two runs over
the same bytes produce byte-identical

output.

An unreadable or missing path is a usage error and goes to stderr in the CLI's
standard error envelope rather than as

findings — nothing was read, so there is
nothing to report about.

**What "valid" does not mean, without `--project`.** The
offline check judges\nthe file against the suite-file contract. It does **not** re-resolve tool names,\nserver references or fixtu

res against a project's live discovery, so a file that
validates here can still fail to run.

#### `--project`: resolving the n

ames against a real project

With `--project`, the command authenticates, resolves the named project, and
checks every determin
istic `toolCall` step against the live tool inventory of\nthe targets the file would run on. Structural findings are unchanged and

you rely on it:

* **Only `toolCall` steps count.** A tool named in prompt text is a hint the
 model may or may not act on, a
nd an `assert` step is an expectation a case may\n legitimately fail at run time. Treating either as a deterministic reference\n
would make a negative test unwritable.\n* **Per target, never over their union.** A file that runs against several\n targets mus
t resolve in all of them; a union would green-light a case that\n fails on two targets out of three.\n* **Auth and network failur
es are command errors, not findings.** \"Your file\n names a tool that does not exist\" and \"we could not look\" send you to two

different places, so they are never reported as the same thing.

A completed live check with unresolved references is a **ve
rdict on the file**\nand exits `1`, like any other contract failure. A failure to authenticate,\nreach the project, or list a serv

er's tools is a command error on stderr.

### `cloud eval export`

Write a hosted eval suite to a local suite file.

| Flag

| Required | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `--suite <id-or-name>` | Yes | Eval suite to export (name or ID) |
| `--project <id-
or-name>` | No | Project the suite belongs to (defaults to the most recently updated project) |\n| `--out <path>` | No | Where to
write (default `.mcpjam/evals/<suite-id>.yaml`) |\n| `--force` | No | Replace an existing file at the output path |\n| `--schema-v
ersion <1\\|2>` | No | Suite-file dialect to write. `1` (the default) spells the count `repetitions` and the rules `checks`; `2` s
pells them `iterations` and `assertions`. Both dialects load. |\n\nThe default path uses the suite's **id**, not its display name:

an id is stable
and path-safe, so a rename does not leave a second file behind.

Like `eval run --file`, export reads `GET /ca
pabilities` first and fetches the\ncases in the vocabulary the deployment advertises; the file it writes is the\nsame either way.

`--schema-version` chooses the file's dialect, the deployment
chooses the wire's vocabulary, and neither decides the other.

Th
e dialect is the author's choice and is never inferred: a file has no\nhandshake with whatever will read it later, so `eval export

` keeps writing
`schemaVersion: "1"` until you ask for `2`.

**Fail-closed.** A suite file cannot express everything a hosted
suite can, and\nthis command refuses rather than writing a file that describes a different test\nthan the dashboard runs. When an
y part of a suite is not representable it emits\n`UNSUPPORTED_SUITE_EXPORT` findings, exits `1`, and writes **no file at all** —\n
not a partial one, not one with a warning comment. Every finding names the field\nit is about, so the command's output is the auth

oritative list; the constructs
that refuse today include:

* several attached project environments, or legacy servers combined

# Create an eval case

> Adds one case to the suite. Both `title` and a non-em
pty `steps` array are required — `steps` is optional on the shared case shape so PATCH can be partial, but a case persisted withou

t executable steps could never run. When `models` is omitted the suite's configured model is used.
